common_name: Amsterdam Forcing Carrot (Fast Early Dutch Baby Carrot)

planting.note: Direct sow in loose, stone-free soil as soon as the ground can be worked; Amsterdam Forcing is bred for very fast, uniform early growth and is a classic choice for the first carrot sowing of spring or for tight succession plantings.

directions: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in loose, well-worked soil in full sun, keeping the surface evenly damp until the slow-to-emerge seedlings appear, then thin to about 2 inches apart. Amsterdam Forcing is a classic Dutch heirloom bred specifically for speed, producing slender, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots with a fine, sweet flavor and almost no core, ready to pull well before slower main-crop carrots. Its small size and rapid growth make it an excellent choice for containers, cold frames, and tight succession sowings every few weeks through the cool season. Harvest young, at finger to baby-carrot size, for the best texture and sweetness, since roots left in the ground too long lose the tenderness that defines the type.

common_name: Kyoto Red Carrot (Kintoki, Japanese New Year Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow into deeply worked, loose soil in mid-to-late summer for a fall and winter harvest; Kyoto Red needs a long, cool growing season to develop its full length and deep color, so it is best sown as a fall crop in zone 9.

directions: Sow seed thinly in deep, loose, stone-free soil in full sun and thin seedlings to 3–4 inches apart, since this variety needs a long, undisturbed taproot run to reach its full 10- to 12-inch length. Kyoto Red, also known as Kintoki carrot, is a traditional Japanese heirloom prized for its striking, uniformly deep red-orange color that holds even after cooking, along with a sweet, dense flesh valued in Japanese New Year dishes and simmered preparations. It grows more slowly than Western carrot types and performs best with a long, cool finish, so a late-summer sowing timed to mature through fall and winter gives the best color and flavor. Harvest once roots reach full size and store dug roots cool and slightly moist for extended keeping.

planting.note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; because Albina Vereduna's roots are pure white, they never stain cutting boards or bleed color into other foods the way red beets do.

directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to 3–4 inches once true leaves appear. Albina Vereduna is an old Dutch heirloom beet that produces round, creamy-white roots with a sweet, mild flavor generally regarded as less earthy than red beets, and because it contains no betalain pigment it can be roasted, pickled, or grated into salads without staining hands, cutting boards, or other ingredients pink. The glossy green tops are also excellent cooked as greens and, lacking red pigment, cook up a cleaner green than the tops of red beet varieties. Keep soil consistently moist for smooth, tender roots and harvest at 2–3 inches across for the best texture, since oversized roots can turn woody.
